lesson.title: The Leibniz Notation That Makes Implicit Differentiation Work
lesson.summary: Writing dy/dx instead of a bare number is what keeps implicit differentiation honest: it records that y is a function of x, not a second independent variable.
lesson.body:
The single piece of notation that trips up most students the first time they see implicit differentiation is this: when you differentiate the term y with respect to x, you do not get 1, and you do not get 0. You get dy/dx. Formally, d/dx[y] = dy/dx by definition, there is nothing to compute; dy/dx is simply the name we give to that derivative, since we do not have an explicit formula for y in terms of x to differentiate directly.

Where the notation earns its keep is on anything more complicated than y by itself. Consider d/dx[y^2]. It is tempting to write 2y, by analogy with d/dx[x^2] = 2x, but that would be wrong: y^2 is a composite expression, the outer operation is squaring and the inner function is y(x), so the chain rule forces a trailing factor of dy/dx: d/dx[y^2] = 2y (dy/dx). Leaving that factor off is the single most common error in this whole topic, and writing dy/dx explicitly, every time, is what stops you from dropping it by accident.

Try xy = 1. The left side is a product of two functions of x, namely x itself and y(x), so it needs the product rule: d/dx[xy] = x (dy/dx) + y (1) = x (dy/dx) + y. The right side, d/dx[1], is 0. So x (dy/dx) + y = 0, which gives dy/dx = -y/x. You can check this immediately, since xy = 1 does solve explicitly: y = 1/x, so dy/dx = -1/x^2. And -y/x = -(1/x)/x = -1/x^2, the same answer.

Why prefer dy/dx over the shorter prime notation y' here? Once an expression involves x, y, and their derivative all at once, y' does not say with respect to which variable the derivative was taken, while dy/dx names both variables explicitly. That bookkeeping matters more and more as equations get longer, and it is exactly the notation you will lean on again once you start solving algebraically for dy/dx and computing second derivatives implicitly.
